# Zechariah 7 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter records an inquiry from a delegation about continuing certain fasts instituted during the exile, and God's answer through Zechariah: fasting not commanded by God, performed with selfish motives, has no value; what God has always required is ethical obedience—justice, mercy, compassion—and their ancestors' refusal of this brought the exile itself.

## v. 1 — The Date of the Prophecy

"In the fourth year of King Darius, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, the month of Chislev."

- **Date:** December 7, 518 B.C. (or early December). This was nearly two years after Zechariah's eight night visions (cf. Zech 1:7), about two years after the temple foundation was laid (Hag 2:10), and about two years before the temple's completion (Ezra 6:15). The temple was roughly halfway completed when this message came. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **Chislev (Kislev):** The Babylonian name for the ninth month (part of November–December). The use of the Babylonian calendar name reflects the post-exilic setting. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html ; https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)

## v. 2 — The Delegation from Bethel

"Now the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech, along with their men, to plead before the LORD."

- **"Bethel":** Ellicott notes that "Bethel" stands for the inhabitants of Bethel (about 10 miles north of Jerusalem), many of whom had returned from exile (Ezra 2:28). There is no instance of "Bethel" (house of God) being used to denote the Temple itself, contra the older English Version rendering "unto the house of God." Constable adds that Bethel had long been associated with apostate worship (1 Kgs 12:29-33; Amos 3:14), so these men would be particularly eager to determine orthodox practice. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **Alternative reading:** Some scholars (cited by Constable, following Baldwin) suggest the names could be transliterated differently: "Bethel-Sharezar" (meaning "house of God, protect the king") and "Regem-melech" (meaning "king's friend") might refer to a single person with a royal title from Darius. Under this view the delegation might have come from Babylon, not Bethel. But Constable thinks the local-from-Bethel view more likely. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **Babylonian names:** Sharezer (or Sarezer) is an Assyrian/Babylonian name meaning "May [the god] protect the king." It appears also in Isaiah 37:38 and Jeremiah 39:3. This suggests these men were born in Babylon during the captivity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **Purpose:** They came "to plead before the LORD" (lit. "to entreat the face of the LORD"), i.e., to seek God's favour and direction through the priests and prophets at the temple. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html)

## v. 3 — The Question about Fasting

"by asking the priests of the house of the LORD of Hosts, as well as the prophets, 'Should I weep and fast in the fifth month, as I have done these many years?'"

- **The fast of the fifth month (Ab, July/August):** Commemorated the burning of the temple by Nebuzaradan. The temple was burned on either the 7th (2 Kgs 25:8-10) or the 10th (Jer 52:12-13) of the fifth month. Ellicott suggests it may have been in flames for three days. Later Jewish tradition (the Mishnah) fixed the fast on the 9th of Ab. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)
- **Why the question now:** The temple rebuilding was well under way (half complete). With the restoration progressing, it seemed natural to ask whether a fast mourning the temple's destruction should continue. Also, 68 of the prophesied 70 years of captivity (Jer 25:11-12) had passed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)
- **The singular "I":** The text uses the first-person singular ("Should I weep"), which Gill explains as the delegation speaking as a corporate body represented by a single voice. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)
- **"These many years":** Refers to the approximately 70 years of exile during which these fasts had been observed. These fasts were not commanded by God in the Law of Moses (only the Day of Atonement fast was commanded, Lev 16:29-34). They were man-made traditions. Yet after 70 years of observance they had taken on a legitimacy of their own. Guzik notes: "They thought, 'We've done this for so many years, we may as well keep doing it.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)
- **"Separating myself":** The Hebrew verb suggests abstaining from food and drink, i.e., fasting. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html)
- **The four exile fasts (mentioned in 8:19):** (1) 10th month, 10th day — beginning of Nebuchadnezzar's siege; (2) 4th month, 17th day — capture of Jerusalem; (3) 5th month, 9th/10th day — burning of temple; (4) 7th month, 3rd day — assassination of Gedaliah. The delegation only asked about the 5th-month fast because it related specifically to the temple. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **Constable raises an important caution:** "What may have appeared to be an innocent question about the propriety of fasting was instead a question fraught with hypocrisy, as YHWH's response puts beyond any doubt. It therefore appears that the query to Zechariah by the Bethelites may not have been so much a matter of piety as it was of posturing." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)

## v. 4 — The Word Comes to Zechariah

"Then the word of the LORD of Hosts came to me, saying."

- This phrase introduces the first of four answer-sections (7:4-7; 7:8-14; 8:1-17; 8:18-23), each marked by the same preamble. It certifies the divine origin of the message—Zechariah did not speak from himself. The first two sections (ch. 7) are negative; the last two (ch. 8) are positive. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html)
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary emphasises that like all true prophets, Zechariah did not claim his messages were of his own design but of supernatural origin, citing 2 Pet 1:21 and 2 Tim 3:16-17. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/zechariah-7.html)

## v. 5 — God's Penetrating Question

"'Ask all the people of the land and the priests, "When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months for these seventy years, was it really for Me that you fasted?"'"

- **"All the people...and the priests":** Though the question came from a delegation from Bethel, the answer is addressed to the whole nation—the issue had widespread implications. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **The seventh month fast:** Commemorated the assassination of Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor (2 Kgs 25:25; Jer 41:1-2). The prophet mentions it here though the delegation only asked about the fifth month, broadening the scope of the reply. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **"Did you at all fast unto Me, even to Me?"** (Gill's rendering): The emphatic repetition ("for Me—for Me") underscores the core issue. Gill says the fast was not according to God's command, not directed to His glory, nor of any profit to Him—it was "nothing to him whether they fasted or not" (cf. Isa 58:3). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)
- **Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic perspective):** God's rebuke is that their fasting had become "indulgent seasons of self-pity instead of a time to genuinely seek God." A few days of fasting cannot make up for a year of living for self. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)
- **"Seventy years":** A round number for the length of the captivity, calculated from the destruction of the temple (586 B.C.) to this moment (518 B.C.), about 68 years. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)

## v. 6 — Eating and Drinking Also Self-Serving

"'And when you were eating and drinking, were you not doing so simply for yourselves?'"

- The point is that neither their fasting nor their feasting was done with reference to God. Both extremes—self-denial and self-indulgence—were done for themselves, not for the Lord. Gill cites 1 Cor 10:31: "whether you eat or drink...do all to the glory of God." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)
- Constable: "Likewise when the people ate and drank they did it for themselves rather than to please the Lord. They were simply perpetuating the selfishness for which former prophets had rebuked their ancestors." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics)** develops this at length: "Whether you fast or feast in your religious services, it is all for 'yourselves; it is not for me, not for me.' ... How much of the popular religion is of this type? The Almighty might well say to the conventional Churches of Christendom—You rear temples, you contribute property, you preach sermons, you offer prayers, you sing hymns; but it 'is not unto me,' it is not to me, it is all self." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/zechariah/7.htm)

## v. 7 — The Words of the Former Prophets

"'Are these not the words that the LORD proclaimed through the earlier prophets, when Jerusalem and its surrounding towns were populous and prosperous, and the Negev and the foothills were inhabited?'"

- **Translation issue:** Ellicott insists the correct rendering is "Are not these the very words which..." (not "Should ye not hear the words..."). The Hebrew construction parallels Haggai 2:5 and Zech 8:17. The LXX reads it correctly: "Are not these the words?" The point is that the ethical demands about to be quoted in vv. 9-10 are not new—they are the very same words the former prophets had proclaimed before the exile. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html)
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** "It is not fasts that Jehovah requires of you, but that ye should keep His precepts given to you at the time when Jerusalem was in its integrity. Had ye done so then, ye would have had no occasion to institute fasts to commemorate its destruction, for it would never have been destroyed." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/7.htm)
- **"The Negev" (the South):** The desert region south of Beersheba, belonging to Judah (Josh 15:21). It was not always desolate—before the exile it was prosperous and inhabited. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)
- **"The foothills" (Shephelah):** The lowland region west of Judah toward the Mediterranean coast (Josh 15:33), a grazing and agricultural area. The returnees had not yet resettled these areas. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **Guzik:** "If their ancestors had been obedient, they would have never needed to fast, and their land wouldn't have been conquered and desolate." Quoting F.B. Meyer: "There is no need to observe the sad anniversaries of our sins and their accompanying punishment, if once we are assured of God's free forgiveness. When He forgives and restores, the need for dwelling on the bitter past is over." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)

## v. 8 — A Second Word from the Lord

"Then the word of the LORD came to Zechariah, saying."

- This introduces the second of the four messages (7:8-14). Gill notes that God here orders Zechariah to repeat what the former prophets had said and to urge the same things on the people which they had previously rejected—the rejection of which had issued in their ruin. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)
- Whedon's Commentary suggests v. 8 may be a repetition of v. 4 and that v. 9 is the natural continuation of v. 7. (From search excerpt, studylight.org/whe)

## v. 9 — The Ethical Demands: Justice, Mercy, Compassion

"'This is what the LORD of Hosts says: "Administer true justice. Show loving devotion and compassion to one another."'"

- **"Execute true judgment" (KJV):** Gill understands this as addressed primarily to judges—to judge righteously according to God's law without respect of persons, passing sentence as the truth of the case required. But it also applies to every member of God's people. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)
- **"True justice" (Heb. mishpat):** Constable notes this is paired with "loving devotion" (Heb. hesed, covenant faithfulness/kindness) and "compassion" (Heb. rahamim). These three terms together form a concise summary of ethical teaching. Constable cites Ellis: "a concise yet comprehensive range of ethical teaching condensed into four pithy utterances." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **Gill:** Mercy and compassion toward a brother in want is "much more acceptable to God than any legal sacrifices, or outward abstinences and humiliations," citing Hosea 6:6 ("I desire mercy, not sacrifice"). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)
- **The Precept Austin summary:** "Conduct denies confession. It is not our hymn singing on Sunday but our action on Monday that is the real test." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah_commentaries)

## v. 10 — Protection of the Vulnerable

"'Do not oppress the widow or the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor. And do not plot evil in your hearts against one another.'"

- **The four vulnerable groups:** Widow, fatherless (orphan), foreigner (alien/stranger), and poor. These are the classic categories of the disadvantaged that the Law of Moses repeatedly protected (e.g., Deut 24:14). Gill notes that such laws were "frequently inculcated among the Jews." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)
- **"Plot evil in your hearts":** Gill observes that even thoughts of evil are sinful and forbidden by God's law, agreeing with Christ's teaching in Matt 5:22 and Lev 19:17. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)
- **Ellicott's grammatical note:** The better translation is "imagine not evil against one another in your heart" (not "let none of you imagine evil against his brother"). The pronoun is objective case here, not nominative as in Zech 8:17. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html)
- **The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** lists the four oppressions to avoid and adds they were "charged to imagine or devise no evil in their hearts against a brother, to seek no revenge," citing Gen 6:5, Lev 19:18, Ps 36:4, Mic 4:1. (From search excerpt, studylight.org/ghb)
- **The NET Bible** translates: "nor should anyone secretly plot evil against his fellow human being." (https://netbible.org/bible/Zechariah+7)

## v. 11 — Refusal, Stubbornness, and Stopped Ears

"'But they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder; they stopped up their ears from hearing.'"

- **"Pulled away the shoulder" (KJV) / "turned a stubborn shoulder":** Ellicott explains this as the image of an ox that refuses to receive the yoke, citing the parallel in Neh 9:29. It pictures willful, stiff-necked rebellion. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html)
- **Guzik sees a progression of rejection:** "It began with simply refusing to heed God, then a self-justifying shrugging of their shoulders, then stopping their ears. It all ends with hearts as hard as flint." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)
- **Gill:** "They gave, or presented, a rebellious shoulder; a refractory one, that slides back, like a backsliding or refractory heifer, that will not admit of the yoke (Hos 4:16)." They could not bear the yoke of the law nor the burden of duty. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)
- **Constable:** "They turned away from Him stubbornly like a rebellious ox, and they put their fingers in their ears so they would not hear Him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)

## v. 12 — Hearts Like Flint

"'They made their hearts like flint and would not listen to the law or to the words that the LORD of Hosts had sent by His Spirit through the earlier prophets. Therefore great anger came from the LORD of Hosts.'"

- **"Adamant stone" (KJV) / "flint" / "diamond":** The Hebrew word *shamir* means a very hard stone. Ellicott explains "adamant" comes from Greek *adámas* ("unconquerable"), originally applied to steel. The NET Bible notes that while many suggest "diamond," diamond was likely unknown to ancient Israel, so probably a hard stone like emery or corundum is in view. The image is of an impenetrably hard heart. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html ; https://netbible.org/bible/Zechariah+7)
- **Gill's striking observation:** Jewish writers said the *shamir* was a worm-like creature so strong it could cut the hardest stones—used by Moses for the temple stones and by Solomon. Gill then adds a gospel note: "as hard as the adamant is, it is to be softened by the blood of a goat, as naturalists say; so the blood of Christ sprinkled on the heart, and a sense of forgiveness of sin by it, will soften the hardest heart." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)
- **"By His Spirit through the former prophets":** Constable notes this is a remarkable doctrine: "the Holy Spirit as mediator of God's word to the prophets, who were themselves its mediators." He cites Baldwin: "Zechariah is the first to record this aspect of the doctrine of the Spirit." This verse is thus significant for the doctrine of the Spirit's inspiration of the prophets (cf. Neh 9:20, 30; 2 Pet 1:21). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **Guzik:** "Zechariah didn't doubt that the Spirit of God genuinely inspired his words and the words of other prophets." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)
- **"Therefore great anger came":** The wrath was not arbitrary but the just response to persistent, willful rejection. Guzik: "When you meet people with hearts like flint, you know they did not become that way overnight. There was a gradual, certain progression to their present place of hardness." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)

## v. 13 — Reciprocal Judgment: God Refuses to Listen

"'And just as I had called and they would not listen, so when they called I would not listen, says the LORD of Hosts.'"

- **The principle of measure-for-measure judgment:** Because they refused to hear God when He called through the prophets, God refused to hear them when they called in their distress. Gill cites Prov 1:24-26. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)
- **Guzik:** "Since God's people refused to listen to God, God would refuse to listen to and answer their prayers. This is just another good reason to stay under the teaching of God's word—so that our prayers will be answered." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)
- **Constable:** "Since the forefathers refused to listen to the Lord's Spirit when He called to them...the Lord refused to listen to them when they called to Him in prayer (cf. Jer 11:11-14)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** "As He (God) had cried to them through the prophets and they obstinately, willfully stopped their ears and hardened their hearts, even so, when they cried in their calamities; In just retribution, He would not hear their cries or prayers." References cited: Prov 1:24-26; Isa 1:15; Jer 11:14; Jer 14:11-12; Mic 3:4. (From search excerpt, studylight.org/ghb)
- **Ellicott's textual note:** The LXX incorrectly translates the verbs as future ("and it shall be"), but the Hebrew uses past tense—the judgment had already occurred in history. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html)

## v. 14 — Scattering and Desolation

"'But I scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations that they had not known, and the land was left desolate behind them so that no one could come or go. Thus they turned the pleasant land into a desolation.'"

- **"Scattered them with a whirlwind":** The image conveys the fierceness of God's wrath and the suddenness and violence of the exile. Guzik cites Clarke: "This refers to the swift victories and cruel conduct of the Chaldeans towards the Jews; they came upon them like a whirlwind; they were tossed to and fro, and up and down, everywhere scattered and confounded." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)
- **"Among all the nations that they had not known":** Gill identifies these as the Babylonians, Medes, and Persians—peoples previously unknown to Israel. Constable connects this to the covenant curses of Deut 28:36-37, 64-68. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
- **"The pleasant land" (or "desirable land" / "fruitful land"):** This refers to the land of Canaan, "a land flowing with milk and honey; the glory of all lands" (Ezek 20:6; Deut 8:7). The NET Bible translates "the fruitful land." The land became desolate so that "no one passed through or returned"—the land was emptied of inhabitants. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm ; https://netbible.org/bible/Zechariah+7)
- **"They turned...into a desolation":** Gill notes this could mean either the Israelites by their iniquities (as the cause) or the Babylonians as instruments of God's vengeance. Both are true in different senses. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm)
- **Guzik's closing application:** "Their disobedience and disregard for God led to scattering and desolation. This is always our fate when we allow religious rituals to take the place of a real relationship and daily obedience towards God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)
- **Constable's concluding quote from Ellis:** "While Zechariah may well not have answered the original enquiry directly, he had nevertheless taken up the very essence of ritual in the heart of the worshiper, which was that the outward form of religious activity was useless and lifeless without an accompanying spirit of obedience, confession and repentance." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)

---

## Denominational Distinctives and Traditions

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik)

Guzik emphasises the heart-motivation behind religious practice and the progressive nature of spiritual hardening. He stresses that fasting and ritual are not wrong in themselves, but become wrong when divorced from a genuine relationship with God and daily obedience. The "progression of rejection" (refusal → shoulder-shrugging → stopped ears → flint-like heart) is presented as a warning applicable to every believer. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-7/)

### Baptist (Gill's Exposition, Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary)

Baptist commentaries emphasise the distinction between man-made traditions and divine commands. Gill repeatedly stresses that these fasts were "not according to the command of God, but an appointment of theirs" and were "nothing to him whether they fasted or not." The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary structures the chapter around the contrast between formal observances and the "spirit of the law" and warns that their forefathers "willfully turned their shoulder and back upon Him, and followed after the ways of heathen gods." Both Baptist sources emphasise that God's judgment was "just retribution"—the principle of sowing and reaping. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/7.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/zechariah-7.html)

### Reformed / Evangelical (Constable's Expository Notes)

Constable follows a dispensational, evangelical approach with careful attention to historical context, Hebrew vocabulary, and intertextual connections. He frames chapters 7–8 as dealing with "the issue of empty ritualism" and stresses that God's purpose is "to impress on the people their need to live righteously in response to their past judgment and future glory." Constable uniquely highlights the theological significance of v. 12 for the doctrine of the Holy Spirit's inspiration of the prophets, citing Baldwin that Zechariah is "the first to record this aspect of the doctrine of the Spirit." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)

### Anglican (Ellicott's Commentary)

Ellicott brings his characteristic attention to Hebrew grammar, textual variants, and the LXX. He provides careful correction of the KJV renderings (e.g., v. 2 "Bethel" as inhabitants, not "house of God"; v. 7 as "are not these the words," not "should ye not hear"; v. 11 "offered a stubborn shoulder" rather than "pulled away"). His approach is philologically rigorous but devotional in application, as when he quotes Moore: "Selfishness is the bane of all true piety, as godliness is its essence." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-7.html)

### Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics — Broader Protestant)

The Pulpit Commentary's homiletical section develops the theme of "Religious Beliefs That Are Right; Religious Services That Are Wrong." It identifies selfish motives as the root problem: "The wrong you had done me was not thought of. Your outrages on morality, on the harmony of the universe, were not thought of at all. How much of the popular religion is of this type?" It also develops the themes of the unity of God's purpose, the mercifulness of God's warnings, and the righteousness of God's judgments. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/zechariah/7.htm)

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible Notes)

The NET Bible provides precise historical and linguistic notes: the date is December 7, 518 B.C.; the *shamir* stone is probably emery or corundum, not diamond (since diamond was likely unknown to ancient Israel); the Shephelah is the region between the coastal plain and the Judean hill country. The NET also notes the Hebrew pronoun switch in v. 13 ("he" to "I") is smoothed for English style. The translation "secretly plot evil" (v. 10) captures the nuance of heart-devising. (https://netbible.org/bible/Zechariah+7)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

*Not found.* Searches of newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org did not return dedicated commentary pages on Zechariah 7 within the search limits. Catholic commentary on this passage is generally consistent with the traditional reading—fasts that are merely external and not joined to justice and charity are rejected by God (see Isaiah 58, which Zechariah 7 closely echoes). This would be the standard Catholic reading, but no specific Catholic page was located.

### The Question of Whether Zechariah Actually Answers

Multiple commentators note a curious feature: Zechariah never gives a direct "yes" or "no" to the question about fasting. Constable quotes Leupold: "Note that the inquiry put by the Bethel committee is not being answered directly. In fact, throughout chapters 7 and 8 no direct answer is offered. The reason is: the question is not an important issue. However, the attitude revealed by that question is of sufficient moment to receive exhaustive treatment." A partial answer does come in 8:18-19 where the fasts will be turned into feasts, but the prophet's main concern is the heart behind the ritual. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-7.html)
